title: PyTorch and NumPy
description: Tensor fluency for ML engineers, the skill every ML coding round assumes and few courses teach directly. Each track starts with a lesson, then has short questions and coding exercises: arrays, views and strides; broadcasting and einsum; indexing, gathers and scatters; autograd; modules and training loops; and the numerics and performance traps that cost hours in real code. Exercises run on a CPU. The PyTorch ones need `torch` on the grading machine, so they run on the board's runners, not in the browser.

tracks.name: Arrays, views and strides
tracks.summary: What an array is in memory (a buffer, a shape, strides and a dtype), and which operations share that buffer.

tracks.name: Broadcasting and einsum
tracks.summary: The two tools that replace most loops in tensor code: broadcasting for elementwise work across shapes, einsum for every kind of contraction.

tracks.name: Indexing, gathers and scatters
tracks.summary: Picking, masking and accumulating by index: the operations behind embeddings, losses, top-k, segment sums and MoE routing.

tracks.name: Autograd
tracks.summary: How PyTorch computes gradients: the graph it records, when it frees it, what `no_grad` and `detach` cut, and how to write a backward by hand.

tracks.name: Modules, optimizers and training loops
tracks.summary: `nn.Module`, the training step in the right order, optimizers written from their update rules, and the layers interviewers ask you to derive.

tracks.name: Numerics and performance
tracks.summary: Float precision, stable formulas, dtypes, randomness and the GPU's asynchrony: the details that make tensor code right and fast.
